what_its_for: Adalimumab-atto is used to reduce inflammation and treat several conditions where your immune system attacks your own body. It is approved for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis (spine arthritis), Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, plaque psoriasis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes swelling and inflammation.
how_to_take: This medicine comes as a liquid injection that you give yourself just under the skin (subcutaneous injection). It is available as a prefilled pen or prefilled syringe. Common injection sites are the front of your thighs or your lower belly (abdomen), but avoid the area 2 inches around your belly button. Rotate injection sites each time so you do not inject in the same spot twice in a row. Let the pen or syringe warm up at room temperature for 15 to 30 minutes before injecting — do not microwave or heat it. Clean the injection site with an alcohol wipe and let it dry before injecting. Do not inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, or hard. Your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist will teach you the proper injection technique before you use it at home.
dosing: The dose depends on your condition and your age. For most adults with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or ankylosing spondylitis, the usual dose is 40 mg injected every other week (every 2 weeks). For Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, your doctor will start you on a higher loading dose, then move to a maintenance dose of 40 mg every other week. For plaque psoriasis, a starting dose of 80 mg is given, followed by 40 mg every other week starting one week after the first dose. Doses for children are based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions exactly — do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember. Then continue on your regular schedule from that new date. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Keep adalimumab-atto in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it, and do not use it if it has been frozen. Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 14 days — write down the date you removed it from the refrigerator and throw it away after 14 days if unused. Do not put it back in the refrigerator once it has been stored at room temperature. Keep all needles, pens, and syringes out of reach of children. Dispose of used pens and syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container — never throw loose needles in the regular trash.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting live vaccines (such as the MMR, chickenpox, or live shingles vaccine) while taking this medicine, as it lowers your immune defenses and live vaccines could cause infection. Tell all your doctors and your pharmacist that you are on this medication before getting any vaccine. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially with serious infections. Avoid taking this medicine if you have an active infection — talk to your doctor first. Limit or avoid activities that expose you to infections when possible. Talk to your doctor before starting any new medications, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, sweating, cough, shortness of breath, burning with urination, or a wound that will not heal; signs of tuberculosis such as a persistent cough, coughing up blood, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat; numbness, tingling, vision changes, or weakness in arms or legs (which could be signs of nerve problems); signs of heart failure such as new or worsening shortness of breath or swelling in your legs or feet; unusual bruising or bleeding; extreme tiredness or yellowing of the skin or eyes (possible liver problems); or any new or unusual lump or bump under the skin. This medication can increase your risk of certain cancers, including lymphoma, so report any unexplained lumps or swollen lymph nodes promptly.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in your symptoms within 2 to 4 weeks of starting treatment. However, it can take 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefit of this medication. Do not stop taking it just because you do not notice results right away. Keep all follow-up appointments with your doctor so they can check how well the medication is working for you.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you take this medicine during pregnancy, your baby should not receive live vaccines for at least 5 months after your last dose during pregnancy. Children: This medicine is approved for use in children 2 years and older for certain conditions; the dose is based on the child's body weight. Elderly patients: Older adults may have a higher risk of infections while taking this medicine; your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: No specific dose adjustments are required, but tell your doctor about any kidney or liver issues you have.
